blogs.title: "Fair Use for Weighted Scales? How Santos v. Kimmel Clarifies Transformative Parodies at Pleading Stage"
blogs.description:
"This post examines how Judge Lohier’s opinion sharpens the transformative‑use test at Rule 12(b)(6). Relying on Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith and Hachette Book Group v. Internet Archive, the Court rejects George Santos’s argument that his Patreon‑type videos were ‘positive’ rather than satirical when viewed by an ordinary observer.

The decision confirms that a plaintiff must show more than intent—it must establish a reasonableness standard based on what such an observer would perceive as commentary or criticism rather than mere duplication.

Because good‑faith defenses such as those once invoked in Harper & Row are now deemed irrelevant when transformed works are judged transformatively enough, Santos’ complaint collapses.

Implications abound for late‑night hosts scoffing former politicians or corporations gambling past user requests—any new parody must already carry persuasive evidence that an audience sees it clearly differently from its source material."

blogs.title: "No Contracts Here! Why Third‑Party Claims Fail Against Digital Platforms"
blogs.description:
"Santos attempts to levy breach‑contract complaints against Jimmy Kimmel via Cameo’s Terms — yet Judge Lohier deems him neither party nor an implied beneficiary.

Illinois law carries a rigid presumption against extending contract benefits to noncontractors unless expressly provided—a principle echoed in Barry v. St. Mary’s Hospital.

At New York state level, any implied agreement requires clear mutual assent; here none exists since Mans’ complaint omits fundamental terms such as offer acceptance or obligation statement.

The ruling therefore eliminates an entire class of lawsuits predicated upon demanding digital platforms honor user requests made outside their signed ToS bundle.

For future litigation involving platforms handling user‑generated requests or custom production services—especially where participants aren’t party—the Handler doctrine reminds us courts will view any claim through sharp lens unless terms explicitly confer benefit."

blogs.title: "Unclaimed Loss Makes Fraudulent Inducement Unviable? Lessons From Santos v. Kimmel About New York Schadenfreude"
blogs.description:
"The Case illustrates how absence of an out‑of‑pocket loss bars fraudulent inducement under New York law.

Under Lama Holding Co. v. Smith­Barney the Court demands demonstrable tangible injury—not merely reputation harm—to support a fraudulent inducement action.

Santos failed even preliminarily here because he offered no evidence he suffered measurable economic damage from says misrepresentation displayed on national television.

The rationales echo Connaughton v.­Chipotle where punitive elements were discarded absent clear economic injury.

Moving forward litigants cannot rely solely on reputational burdons when alleging fraud against media personalities;
they must align their pleadings with statutory requirements demanding concrete financial harm—or look toward competing notions such as malicious misrepresentation under defamation statutes instead."
